title: Accountability, Trust, and Quality Assurance in AI-Augmented Regulatory Document Production: Findings from a Three-Year Field Deployment in US Immigration
author: Liz Meira Miossi

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Human oversight: Accountability is not effective control
st.an: The source accepts that accountability alone does not ensure effective oversight and materially extends the cluster with field evidence from immigration-document production. It reports ambiguous responsibility, automation complacency, error-derived controls, and complementary human and automated review, while its observational design limits causal and comparative claims.
qs: When AI participates in production, the answer becomes ambiguous.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core supervised-copilot and sociotechnical deployment proposition, then materially extends it with 38 months of field evidence from regulatory petition production. It finds that acceptable quality requires combined human and automated review and develops a concrete framework for allocating responsibility, calibrating trust and evolving quality standards across the workflow.
qs: Neither automated systems nor human reviewers alone achieve acceptable quality; their combination does.

These findings suggest that the central challenge of deploying AI in high-stakes regulatory document production is not primarily technical (how to make the AI more accurate) but sociotechnical (how to distribute responsibility, calibrate trust, and evolve quality standards in collaboration between human operators and automated systems).

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core view that legal AI requires selective, human-led deployment and materially extends it with longitudinal field observations on how verification degrades through complacency, how automated and expert review catch different failures, and how QA and workflow controls must evolve after deployment. Its single-domain, single-operator, retrospective design limits generalisation but does not undermine alignment.
qs: Regulatory frameworks that mandate human oversight without addressing the complacency dynamic may create a false sense of security.

These findings suggest that the central challenge of deploying AI in high-stakes regulatory document production is not primarily technical (how to make the AI more accurate) but sociotechnical (how to distribute responsibility, calibrate trust, and evolve quality standards in collaboration between human operators and automated systems).

kp.k: Longitudinal deployment provides situated evidence, not experimental proof
kp.d: Miossi reports a retrospective, observational deployment spanning 38 months, March 2023 to May 2026, predominantly producing EB2-NIW petition business plans. The abstract reports over 340 cases; the methodology describes approximately 350 documents, comprising 172, 170 and 5 cases across three operations. Approximately 95% were EB2-NIW. The author was designer, primary operator and researcher; single-domain, single-operator and model-specific limitations constrain generalisation, while historical comparisons cannot isolate automation from learning, case complexity or regulatory changes.
qs: The study period spans 38 months (March 2023 through May 2026) across three sequential and overlapping operations in the same regulatory domain (US immigration petition documents).
The deployed system processed approximately 350 regulatory petition documents across three operations:
We cannot isolate the effect of automation from confounding variables such as operator learning, client complexity variation, and regulatory environment changes.

kp.k: Production accelerates, but process redesign preceded AI gains
kp.d: The paper reports an industry baseline of 15 to 60 days per document, manual optimisation from 21 to 5 days, approximately 7 days with AI-assisted research, approximately 24 hours of work during co-drafting, and a current orchestrated average of 3 days with a 1-day minimum. These are historical phase comparisons, with production times estimated from operational records. The author emphasises that the first major efficiency improvement occurred before AI introduction.
qs: Production time evolved from an industry baseline of 15 to 60 days per document to a current average of 3 days, with a minimum of 1 day.
The first major efficiency improvement (from 21 days to 5 days) occurred before any AI was introduced, through process redesign alone.
Production time per document by phase (estimated from operational records)

kp.k: Orchestration changes drafting into gated review work
kp.d: The architecture combines a 7-stage Client Investigation pipeline, a financial modelling module and a 5-stage Business Plan pipeline. A locked CI Final supplies downstream information, intermediate artifacts permit inspection, and eight human decision points retain operator approval. The human role shifts from drafter and researcher to editor, reviewer and quality guardian rather than disappearing. Corrections are made to pipeline prompts, rules or logic to propagate fixes across future cases.
qs: The output is a locked "CI Final" document that serves as the single source of truth for all downstream generation.
Eight human decision points are embedded in the pipeline.
Errors are corrected at the pipeline level (in prompts, rules, or system logic), never in individual documents.
These gates exist because the regulatory and ethical responsibility for document quality rests with the human operator, not with the automated system.

kp.k: Error reductions differ sharply across failure categories
kp.d: Reported factual inconsistencies declined from approximately 30% of initial outputs to below 5% after rule codification; regulatory compliance violations declined from approximately 20% to approximately 8%; formatting errors declined from 40%+ to below 3%. Narrative coherence failures remained approximately 15% across phases and showed the least improvement from automated QA. These are deployment observations, not independently benchmarked model error rates.
qs: Frequency: observed in approximately 30% of initial pipeline outputs before QA rules were codified. After codification, frequency dropped below 5%.

Frequency: observed in approximately 20% of initial pipeline outputs. After iterative rule codification (11 named quality injection rules, each derived from a specific failure), frequency decreased to approximately 8%.
Frequency: observed in approximately 15% of pipeline outputs across all phases. This category has shown the least improvement from automated QA, remaining relatively stable.

Frequency: HIGH in early pipeline versions (observed in 40%+ of outputs). After programmatic checks (anti-leak validation for internal terminology, section numbering verification), frequency dropped to below 3%.

kp.k: Automation concentrates human accountability on difficult judgments
kp.d: The author assigns factual consistency and formatting primarily to system design, compliance to shared system/operator responsibility, and narrative coherence primarily to the operator. Automation therefore leaves humans responsible for the most expertise-intensive judgments, making their residual work cognitively harder. Drawing on Elish's moral crumple zone concept, Miossi identifies implications for operator training, workload assessment and role design.
qs: Automation delegates the easiest-to-detect failure categories (A and D) to the system while shifting the hardest-to-detect categories (B and C) to the human operator.
The result is that the operator's job becomes cognitively harder, not easier, after automation.
This has direct implications for training, workload assessment, and role design in AI-augmented regulatory document production.

kp.k: Trust progresses from scrutiny toward complacency risk
kp.d: The retrospective single-operator model distinguishes productive distrust in months 1–8, approximately cases 1–60; calibrated confidence in months 9–18, approximately cases 61–180; and complacency risk in months 19–38, approximately cases 181–340+. Early review sometimes exceeded manual production time and generated approximately 40% of current quality injection rules. Selective review subsequently delivered the highest productivity and lowest error rates, but familiarity later allowed errors into delivered documents. The author treats these as approximate qualitative phases and recommends multi-operator validation.
qs: Phase boundaries are approximate and reflect qualitative shifts in operational behavior, not discrete events.
Revision time frequently exceeded the time that manual production would have required.
Review shifted from "read everything" to "verify critical points."
Extended familiarity with the pipeline generated a tendency to accept output without deep review.

kp.k: Complacency incidents motivate deliberate friction and external review
kp.d: Documented missed errors included a position-title inconsistency, a revenue model using gross sale price rather than net development margin and producing profit margins above 50%, and Portuguese text in an English client document. An external attorney caught the financial anomaly. Responses included mandatory go/no-go gates, error-log review, periodic independent attorney review, forced delays and full-document review requirements. The author recommends these as safeguards against declining vigilance, while proposing future research to measure their effects.
qs: The operator approved the financial section without catching the anomaly because the overall financial narrative "sounded right."
This error was only detected when a third-party attorney reviewer flagged it.

Examples from our deployment include mandatory binary gates (the system cannot proceed without explicit operator confirmation), forced delays between pipeline stages (preventing rapid, unreviewed approval), and periodic full-document review requirements (rather than checkpoint-only review).
In high-stakes domains, some friction is not an inefficiency to be eliminated; it is a safety feature to be preserved.

kp.k: Quality rules develop through documented production failures
kp.d: The paper reports over 160 codified rules across 9 pipeline stages, each tracing to a production failure rather than advance specification. Rules address factual integrity (approximately 35%), compliance (25%), consistency (20%), internal terminology leaks (10%) and process boundaries (10%). Systemic errors trigger root-cause analysis, prompt-level rules, testing against the triggering case and documented provenance. Two rule conflicts required explicit precedence or revision, illustrating continuing maintenance rather than a finished specification.
qs: The quality assurance framework in the deployed pipeline currently comprises over 160 codified rules distributed across 9 pipeline stages.
None of these rules were specified before deployment. Every rule traces to a documented failure in a real production case.
The rule is tested against the case that triggered it to verify that the error would now be prevented.
We documented two instances of rule conflict and their resolution.

kp.k: Automated checks and human judgment provide complementary safeguards
kp.d: Miossi reports that automated checks better detected cross-section factual inconsistencies and formatting defects, while humans better detected narrative weaknesses and subtle regulatory deficiencies. External immigration attorneys found coherence problems missed by both operator and automation, whereas automated QA found financial inconsistencies attorneys missed. The author formulates a complementarity principle requiring structured allocation of review responsibilities, with external review calibrating both; this is an observational finding rather than a controlled comparison of review regimes.
qs: Across all phases of the study, we observed a consistent pattern: automated QA and human review detect different types of failures, with limited overlap.
Simultaneously, the external reviewers identified Category C issues (narrative coherence, argumentative strength) that neither the automated QA nor the operator had flagged.

The automated system handles factual consistency and formatting (Categories A and D). The human operator handles narrative coherence and regulatory compliance judgment (Categories B and C). External review provides a calibration check on both.

kp.k: Drafting automation relocates rather than eliminates production bottlenecks
kp.d: Automated stages execute in approximately 22 minutes, but overall production remains constrained by client questionnaires and confirmations, operator approvals and external quality assessments. The author argues that efficiency gains plateau at this human-interaction bottleneck, making questionnaire design, review interfaces and feedback processes the next targets for improvement rather than further AI acceleration.
qs: Automation resolved this bottleneck (pipeline execution time is approximately 22 minutes for the automated stages). But the bottleneck did not disappear; it migrated.

The current bottleneck is the human-system interaction: the time for the client to complete the questionnaire and respond to confirmations, the time for the operator to review and approve intermediate outputs, and the time for external reviewers to provide quality assessments.
Further optimization requires improving the design of human interactions (questionnaire design, review interfaces, feedback mechanisms), not further AI capability.

kp.k: Regulatory advocacy requires more than technically correct content
kp.d: The paper distinguishes generating petition arguments from AI-assisted adjudication: the system supports advocacy to a human decision-maker rather than deciding legal status. Petition quality combines codified requirements with interpretive persuasion under Matter of Dhanasar. The author argues that narrative coherence, strategic framing and adaptation to the adjudicator's framework are precisely where human expertise remains most necessary, and recommends distinguishing advocacy from adjudication in computational-law research.
qs: The AI system does not adjudicate; it advocates.
In advocacy, the document must be persuasive, not merely correct.
Persuasion requires narrative coherence, strategic framing, and adaptation to the evaluator's decision framework (in this case, Matter of Dhanasar).
These are precisely the dimensions where automated QA performs worst and human judgment is most essential.

kp.k: Governance should maintain oversight and learn from supervised deployment
kp.d: Interpreting its findings alongside the EU AI Act and NIST AI RMF, the paper argues that requiring human oversight is insufficient unless review quality is actively maintained over time. It recommends supervised regulatory sandboxes followed by formalisation of empirically derived QA rules, asserting that advance prescriptive standards may be ineffective. These are governance arguments extrapolated from the deployment; the study has no experimental control establishing superiority over top-down specification.
qs: Regulatory frameworks that mandate human oversight without addressing the complacency dynamic may create a false sense of security.
Effective oversight requires not only the presence of a human reviewer but active mechanisms to maintain review quality over extended operation.

A regulatory approach that requires supervised deployment periods (regulatory sandboxes) followed by formalization of empirically derived rules may produce better outcomes than prescriptive standards.

kp.k: Privacy and stakeholder transparency remain consequential design questions
kp.d: Immigration documents combine personal, financial and status information with potentially severe consequences for petitioners. Although intermediate artifacts make the pipeline inspectable to the operator, the author describes it as opaque to petitioners and adjudicators. Future work asks whether AI assistance should be disclosed to petitioners and whether adjudicators should distinguish AI-generated from manually produced documents; these are open ethical and design questions, not established disclosure requirements.
qs: Immigration petition documents contain personal identification, financial records, employment history, educational credentials, and immigration status information.

Our current pipeline is transparent to the operator but opaque to two critical stakeholders: the petitioner (whose immigration case depends on the document) and the adjudicator (the USCIS officer who evaluates it).
Should petitioners be informed that their document was produced with AI assistance? Should adjudicators be able to distinguish AI-generated from manually produced documents?

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Miossi reports faster immigration-support document production, while distinguishing AI acceleration from prior process redesign and predicting a plateau at human-interaction bottlenecks.
pts.d: For business plans supporting US immigration petitions, Miossi reports a current average production time of three days, a one-day minimum, and approximately 22 minutes for automated pipeline stages, compared with a stated third-party industry baseline of 15–60 days. She explicitly attributes the initial reduction from 21 to five days to pre-AI process redesign. She argues that automation moves the bottleneck from drafting to client responses, operator verification and approvals, and external expert review; further gains therefore require better human-interaction design rather than additional model capability.

pts.k: Miossi claims automation changes the operator from drafter to reviewer and concentrates human responsibility on the most cognitively demanding errors.
pts.d: Her four-category taxonomy distinguishes factual inconsistency, regulatory compliance violation, narrative coherence failure, and formatting/structural errors. She assigns factual consistency and formatting primarily to system design, regulatory compliance jointly to system and operator, and narrative coherence primarily to the operator. The claimed change is not elimination of professional responsibility but concentration of residual responsibility in expert judgment. These are the author's accountability assignments, not reported legal determinations of liability.

pts.k: Miossi claims reliable regulatory document production requires complementary automated checks, human verification, and external expert review—not autonomous substitution.
pts.d: Automated checks are said to outperform people on cross-document field consistency and formatting, while people outperform those checks on persuasive coherence and nuanced regulatory fit. External immigration attorneys identify issues missed by both the operator and automated system. Miossi distinguishes AI-generated advocacy from adjudication: the pipeline produces arguments for human decision-makers rather than deciding petitions. Eight human decision points embed an augmentation model even in the fully orchestrated production phase.

pts.k: Miossi claims sustained use can turn calibrated trust into complacency, making human oversight insufficient without mechanisms that maintain vigilance.
pts.d: She describes productive distrust, calibrated confidence, and complacency risk as successive phases of her operator experience. Initial intensive verification sometimes consumed more time than manual drafting; selective verification subsequently increased productivity; later familiarity allowed errors into delivered documents. She interprets complacency as a predictable consequence of reliability and recommends mandatory gates, deliberate friction, error logs, periodic full-document review, and independent expert review. The proposed general trajectory and safeguards extend beyond the individual episodes reported.

pts.k: Miossi claims effective AI quality rules emerge from production failures and require continuous revision; she proposes supervised deployment as a basis for standards.
pts.d: She reports over 160 rules across nine stages, each traced to a production failure. The development cycle comprises detection, root-cause analysis, prompt-level requirements or prohibitions, testing against the triggering case, and documentation. Pipeline-level corrections are intended to propagate fixes to future cases. She argues that this bottom-up process is more effective than specifying rules in advance and suggests regulatory sandboxes before formalizing standards. The standards proposal is an implication drawn from deployment experience, not a reported comparison of regulatory regimes.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence is a retrospective, observational field deployment with operational records, error logs, rule histories, and the designer-operator's experience.
pts.d: Miossi reports more than 340 cases over a stated 38-month period, with operation-level counts of 172, 170, and five, and approximately 95% EB2-NIW work. Production times are estimates from operational records. Error categories were iteratively coded, beginning with the first 50 cases. Other materials include 11 named quality-injection rules, ten technical incidents, two rule conflicts, workflow logs, and self-observation notes. Historical and cross-phase comparisons support the efficiency claims; no randomized control group or model benchmark is presented. The author identifies her combined designer, primary operator, and researcher role and includes external attorney assessments as a mitigation.

pts.k: Reported error frequencies and attorney comparisons underpin the claims about quality improvement and complementary review.
pts.d: Miossi reports factual inconsistencies in approximately 30% of initial outputs, falling below 5% after rules; regulatory compliance failures falling from approximately 20% to 8%; narrative coherence failures remaining around 15% across phases; and formatting errors falling from over 40% to below 3%. These figures concern pipeline outputs, not petition approval rates or adjudicated liability. Comparative attorney assessments reportedly found coherence problems missed internally, while automated checks found financial inconsistencies attorneys missed. The paper characterizes these as production observations rather than a controlled comparison of review methods.

pts.k: Specific missed errors and retrospective self-observation support the trust claim; production failures and documented rule conflicts support the evolving-QA claim.
pts.d: Complacency examples include inconsistent position titles, a revenue model using gross sale price instead of net development margin and generating profit margins above 50%, and Portuguese text appearing in an English client document. An external attorney detected the financial-model problem, prompting a new classification rule. Trust phases were derived retrospectively rather than measured using validated trust instruments. QA evidence includes rules tested against their triggering cases and two conflicts resolved by clarifying the boundary between business-plan production and attorney-process work. Foundational trust and accountability literature supplies interpretive framing; the author's own deployment supplies the claimed findings.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The reported changes concern March 2023–May 2026; the fully orchestrated workflow belongs to 2025–2026 and trust-phase boundaries are approximate.
pts.d: The paper calls the deployment 38 months. Its production sequence runs from manual process optimization in March–October 2023, through AI-assisted research from October 2023 and co-drafting in 2024–early 2025, to orchestration in 2025–2026. The trust model assigns productive distrust to months 1–8, calibrated confidence to months 9–18, and complacency risk to months 19–38. Governance proposals, predicted efficiency plateaus, and cross-domain possibilities have no fixed future deadline.

pts.k: Miossi limits the findings to one domain, operator, and model-dependent deployment, and conditions generalization on replication.
pts.d: The source explicitly qualifies causal attribution: operator learning, varying case complexity, and regulatory changes accompany automation. Its human-review claims concern this pipeline's combination of generative stages, field comparisons, keyword checks, and expert review. Multi-operator studies and formal trust measurements are proposed to test whether the trust trajectory generalizes. Replication in financial compliance, pharmaceutical submissions, or patent petitions is future work, not an observed result.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The directly affected groups are immigration-document providers and operators, reviewing immigration attorneys, petitioners, and human adjudicators; wider implications concern training and governance.
pts.d: The deployment covers a document department within an immigration services firm, a co-founded venture, and a new operation—not the legal market as a whole. Operators move toward expert verification and quality maintenance, with greater cognitive demands and complacency risks. Immigration attorneys provide independent judgment and review. Petitioners receive documents more quickly but remain exposed to errors affecting immigration status, career, and family life, while supplying highly sensitive information. USCIS adjudicators remain the decision-makers receiving the arguments. Miossi also addresses regulators and system designers through proposals for maintained oversight and experience-derived standards. She makes no concrete forecast of lawyer headcount, fees, firm profitability, or market share.
